text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Revised figures from Statistics Sweden give a new picture of the nation's recent economic history, showing it to be much stronger than previously thought. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) rose more in both 1994 and 1995 than previously reported at 3.3 percent and 3.6 percent respectively.
- Swiss/Swedish engineering group ABB reported a higher profit for the first nine months of 1996 but says it is aiming for a better result next year.
- Former tennis player Bjorn Borg is reported to be close to bankruptcy with his creditors filing against him.
- The Swedish goverment is to take a fresh look at planned chnages to unemployment benefits after a backbench revolt in parliament.

- The country's Volvo car dealers made almost as much money in 1995 as the car division of Volvo itself, even though new car sales were depressed during the year. None of the Volvo dealership chains made a loss last year.

- Patients in the Stockholm county health district who are forced to wait for more than three months for certain types of operation have the right to demand treatment at other hospitals in the country, health authorority auditors say.

- Swedish industry has offered to finance the closing of the nuclear power stations in Ignalina in Lithuania, and Sosnovy Bor near St Petersburg on condition that Sweden nuclear stations can remain active as long as they are technically sound, the paper reports.
- Gas company AGA's president Marcus Storch hands over the job to Lennart Selander. He has been with the company 28 years.
- Sweden's five leading banks are joining Visa International in the trial launch of a Europe-wide Internet-based electronic payments system scheduled to begin in the first quarter of next year.
